summary: Idaho Code § 63-3024A sets the food tax credit (formerly the grocery credit) at $155 per person for tax year 2025 and each year after. The credit is refundable: any part above tax due is paid out as a refund. The household is one 56-year-old resident filer with no dependents. Nothing triggers proration: the head is not SNAP-eligible and no incarceration is listed. That gives $155. The engine awarded the full $155 base credit for all 12 months, which matches the law. The consensus answer of $0 rests on claims that the credit is nonrefundable, repealed or phased out, and all three are wrong. The 2026 bills that would have changed the credit (HB 605 and HB 633, which would have repealed it) were only printed and filed, so neither became law.

summary: California's refundable credits for this single 28-year-old with no children come only from CalEITC. R&TC §17052 lets childless filers claim from age 18, and the §17052(o) extended phaseout runs to about $32,900 for 2025. Under IRC §32(a)(2)(B), the phaseout uses the greater of AGI ($22,535) or earned income. With the 2025 parameters, the latest published before the freeze, the credit is 0.85 × [0.0543 × ~$5,451 − ~1.0779% × (AGI − $5,451)] ≈ $95.15 at the FTB table midpoint, which matches the engine's $95.15. The engine counts earned income as $17,443 instead of $14,665 because it does not subtract the traditional 401(k) deferral, as §32(c)(2)(A)(i) requires. That does not change the result: both figures are past the phase-in, and AGI sets the phaseout. The $0 consensus applied the federal childless cutoff and missed the §17052(o) extension. The 2026 CCPI indexing (about 3.4%, giving roughly $105) was published only after the 2026-07-03 freeze, so the reference rests on law published before the freeze.
